summary: The note describes the monarchy of the United Kingdom as a constitutional monarchy covering the UK, its dependencies and overseas territories, with Queen Elizabeth II as monarch since 1952. It outlines the sovereign's official residences (Buckingham Palace, Windsor Castle, Palace of Holyroodhouse, St James's Palace and others) and private properties. It also traces the monarchy's history from medieval kingdoms through the Civil War, the Commonwealth and Restoration, to the union with Scotland and Ireland.
one_line: Overview of the British monarchy's constitutional role, royal residences, and its history from medieval kingdoms through the Commonwealth to the United Kingdom.
key_facts: The monarchy of the United Kingdom is a constitutional monarchy covering the United Kingdom, its dependencies and its overseas territories.
Queen Elizabeth II ascended the throne on the death of her father, King George VI, on 6 February 1952.
Buckingham Palace in London is the sovereign's official London residence and the site of most state banquets, investitures and royal christenings.
Windsor Castle is described as the largest occupied castle in the world and is used principally at weekends, Easter and during Royal Ascot.
The Palace of Holyroodhouse in Edinburgh is the sovereign's official residence in Scotland, and the monarch stays there for at least one week each year.
Whitehall was destroyed by fire in 1698, leading to a shift to St James's Palace as the main royal residence.
Buckingham Palace replaced St James's Palace as the monarch's primary London residence in 1837, though St James's remains the senior palace.
Foreign ambassadors are accredited to the Court of St James's, and the Palace is the site of the meeting of the Accession Council.
Royal palaces belong to the Crown, are held in trust for future rulers, and cannot be sold by the monarch.
Sandringham House in Norfolk and Balmoral Castle in Aberdeenshire are privately owned by the Queen.
Charles I was executed in 1649, leading to the overthrow of the English monarchy and the establishment of the Commonwealth of England.
In 1653, Oliver Cromwell seized power and declared himself Lord Protector, refusing the title of king.
Charles II returned to Britain and the monarchy was restored in 1660.
England was conquered by the Normans in 1066.
The Act of Settlement 1701 excluded Roman Catholics, or those who married them, from succession to the English throne.
In 1707, England and Scotland merged to create the Kingdom of Great Britain, and in 1801 the Kingdom of Ireland joined to create the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland.
The British Empire covered a quarter of the world's surface at its greatest extent in 1921.
